## What reaches each copy? {#part-recap}

A recap of L13: five ways of keeping a copy of a table up to date, after two fast changes and one delete.

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: false
---

## A ticket app stores seat reservations in a table. A separate copy of the table is updated by the method named in each row. Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

**1.** The ticket API writes seat 22A as "held".<br>**2.** If the copy uses polling, a poll runs here.<br>**3.** The ticket API writes seat 14C as "held".<br>**4.** The ticket API updates seat 14C to "sold".<br>**5.** A cleanup job deletes 22A directly from the table. It does not call the API, write an outbox row or update a copy.<br>**6.** If the copy uses polling, the next poll runs here. If it uses the nightly export, the export runs here and replaces the whole copy.<br><br>Assume every call succeeds, each copy applies what it receives once and in the order the changes were made, and a delete that reaches a copy removes the row. Which of seat 14C's statuses reach each copy during these steps?

- Export the whole table every night :: "sold" only
  > At step 6 the table holds 14C only as "sold", and the export copies the table as it is then.
- Poll the table every 5 minutes on an updated-at column :: "sold" only
  > The poll at step 6 reads 14C as it is then, "sold". It does not see "held".
- Ticket API writes an outbox row in the same transaction as each change :: "held", then "sold"
  > Steps 3 and 4 each commit with their own outbox row, so the copy applies "held" and then "sold".
- Read the table's change stream :: "held", then "sold"
  > The stream records both committed changes, in order for one item.
- Ticket API writes each change to the table and then to the copy, in two separate calls :: "held", then "sold"
  > Here both copy calls succeed, in order. A single transaction does not cover both writes, so in general a call can fail, or two calls can arrive in a different order.
- :: "held" only
  > The export and the poll read the table at step 6, after "sold". The other three ways apply "held" and then "sold".

## A ticket app stores seat reservations in a table. A separate copy of the table is updated by the method named in each row. Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

**1.** The ticket API writes seat 22A as "held".<br>**2.** If the copy uses polling, a poll runs here.<br>**3.** The ticket API writes seat 14C as "held".<br>**4.** The ticket API updates seat 14C to "sold".<br>**5.** A cleanup job deletes 22A directly from the table. It does not call the API, write an outbox row or update a copy.<br>**6.** If the copy uses polling, the next poll runs here. If it uses the nightly export, the export runs here and replaces the whole copy.<br><br>Assume every call succeeds, each copy applies what it receives once and in the order the changes were made, and a delete that reaches a copy removes the row. After step 6, once each consumer has caught up, is seat 22A in each copy?

- Export the whole table every night :: 22A is not in the copy
  > The export at step 6 replaces the copy with the table, which no longer holds 22A.
- Poll the table every 5 minutes on an updated-at column :: 22A is in the copy
  > The poll at step 2 copied 22A. A deleted row does not match any updated-at query, so the poll at step 6 does not learn about the delete.
- Ticket API writes an outbox row in the same transaction as each change :: 22A is in the copy
  > Step 1 wrote an outbox row for 22A, so the copy has it. The cleanup job did not write one, so the delete never reaches the copy.
- Read the table's change stream :: 22A is not in the copy
  > The stream carries 22A's "held" and then its delete, whoever made it, so the consumer removes 22A.
- Ticket API writes each change to the table and then to the copy, in two separate calls :: 22A is in the copy
  > Step 1 wrote 22A to the copy too. The cleanup job did not use the API or update the copy, so the dual write never sends the delete.
- :: 22A is in the copy, marked deleted
  > That needs the copy to keep a deleted marker, and here a delete that reaches a copy removes the row. The export and the change stream remove 22A, and the other three ways never learn about the delete.
```


## Queue, topic and log: which kind of message broker fits each consumer {#part-brokers}

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## A food-delivery app sends order events through AWS and does not store them in a table. For each need, choose the one option that should carry the events, without combining options. Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- Each new order is assigned to one of four kitchen printers :: Queue
  > A queue, such as Amazon SQS, gives each delivery to one consumer, which deletes the message when it is done. Four printers sharing one queue split the orders between them. A standard queue can deliver a message again, so a printer may see a repeat. A topic with each printer subscribed would copy every order to all four.
- A cancelled order must reach the courier app, the customer app and billing as it happens, each with its own copy, and they do not read it again later :: Topic
  > A topic, such as Amazon SNS, copies each message to every subscriber. On one shared queue, the three consumers would take messages away from each other, and each delivery of a cancel would go to only one of them. A log could also give each consumer every event, but it would keep events that nobody here reads again.
- A new fraud model, started today, must also read every order from the three days before it started, including orders other workers have already handled :: Log
  > A log, such as Kinesis Data Streams, keeps every event for its retention period, whether anyone has read it or not. It can replay the three days for a new consumer if its retention was already at least three days, and Kinesis keeps 24 hours by default. A topic does not deliver messages from before the subscription, and a queue does not keep messages after its workers delete them.
- After a bug, the delivery-time service reads the last two hours again, still within retention :: Log
  > Reading again is a replay: the consumer moves its offset, its position in the log, back two hours and reads again. A queue's worker deleted each message when it was done, and a topic does not keep anything once delivered.
- Ten workers share sending receipts, one receipt per order :: Queue
  > Each delivery goes to one of the ten workers, which deletes the message when the receipt is sent. The workers share the messages, which DDIA calls load balancing. A redelivery can still send a second receipt, which Q2 deals with. A topic with each worker subscribed would send ten receipts per order.
- A refunds service, beside billing and the courier app, wants only the cancelled orders, as they happen, and never reads them again :: Topic
  > The refunds service is one more subscriber on the topic that carries the cancelled orders, with a filter policy, a rule that passes it only the cancels. Each subscriber still gets its own copy of what it asked for, and the events do not need to be kept for replay.
- :: Nightly export
  > The app does not store these events in a table, so a table export cannot carry them.
- :: Dual write
  > The app would write each event once for each consumer itself, and a transaction does not cover those writes. One write can fail, or two writes can arrive in a different order, so the copies can disagree. A broker takes one write from the producer and serves the consumers from there.
```
